passages.t: A lamb every morning and every evening
passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “Command the Israelites and say to them: See that you present to Me at its appointed time the food for My offerings by fire, as a pleasing aroma to Me” (verse 2).

The first offering is the one that never stops. Each day two year-old lambs are to be offered. “Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight” (verse 4). With each goes a grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil and a drink offering (verses 5-7).

“This is a regular burnt offering established at Mount Sinai as a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
A new generation has been counted and a new leader named. Now the book sets out the pattern of worship Israel is to keep once it lives in the land. Chapters 28 and 29 make one calendar. It begins with what happens every day and moves outward to the great feasts.

Most of these days were already commanded in Exodus and Leviticus. Those passages spoke mainly of what the people were to do: rest, gather and rejoice. These chapters speak of what the priests are to offer at the altar for the whole nation.

The placing of the calendar is an act of hope. God speaks of harvests and feast days in a land Israel does not yet hold, as if the settling of it were already certain. The offerings call for grain, olive oil and wine, the produce of fields and vineyards that the people do not yet own.

The daily offering is the base of everything. The Hebrew word for ‘regular’ is tamid, which means continual, and in later Jewish tradition this offering was known simply as the Tamid. Every day began and ended with it. A burnt offering was burned whole on the altar. Nothing was kept back by the priest or the worshiper. Day by day the nation gave itself to God at the start and at the close.

A modern reader may stumble at the words ‘the food for My offerings’. Temples across the ancient Near East served daily meals to the images of their gods, and texts from Mesopotamia and Egypt describe the menus. Israel's worship shares some of the vocabulary. But there was no image in Israel's sanctuary to be fed, and a psalm has God say plainly that he needs nothing: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 50:12). The language of food and of a pleasing aroma is the language of welcome and of fellowship. It does not mean that God was hungry.
passages.later:
A psalm sets prayer beside the evening lamb: “May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering” (Psalm 141:2).

The phrase ‘pleasing aroma’ first appears after the flood, when Noah offered a sacrifice (Genesis 8:21). Paul uses the picture of Christ, who ‘gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God’ (Ephesians 5:2).

After the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70 the offerings ceased. Jewish worship was reshaped around prayer, with the daily services understood as answering to the times of the daily offerings.
passages.asks: Israel's day began and ended with an offering that never changed. Ask how your own day begins and ends, and what you give your first and last attention to. And ask what small, steady act of worship you could keep every day, whether or not you feel like it.

passages.happening:
On the Sabbath two more lambs are offered. “This is the burnt offering for every Sabbath, in addition to the regular burnt offering and its drink offering” (verse 10).

At the start of each month the offering is larger: two bulls, a ram and seven lambs, each with its grain and wine, and a goat as a sin offering (verses 11-15).
passages.hearers:
One phrase holds the calendar together: ‘in addition to the regular burnt offering’. It comes again and again through both chapters. Nothing replaces the daily lamb. Every special day is laid on top of it. The calendar is built in layers: the day, the week, the month, and then the year.

The Sabbath doubles the ordinary day. Two lambs are offered every day, and two more on the seventh. The day of rest was marked at the altar by more worship and not by less.

Israel's months followed the moon, and each began when the new moon appeared. The first day of the month was a small feast, with trumpets blown over the offerings (10:10). Marking the new moon set the whole month before God at its start.

The offerings are carefully measured. Each animal comes with flour, oil and wine, and the amounts rise with the size of the animal: least for a lamb, more for a ram, most for a bull. Bread, oil and wine were the staples of the land. The offerings brought the fruit of Israel's farms to God along with its flocks.
passages.later:
Isaiah looks ahead to a day when the same rhythm will gather all peoples: “From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me” (Isaiah 66:23).

Paul tells Christians not to let anyone judge them over such days: ‘a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ’ (Colossians 2:16-17). Christians differ on how the Sabbath command applies now, as the note on 15:32-36 sets out.
passages.asks: Every week and every month in Israel began with something set apart for God. Ask what marks the turn of your week or your month. And ask whether your rest is filled with more of God, or only with less work.

passages.t: Passover and the Feast of Weeks
passages.happening:
“The fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD’s Passover” (verse 16). From the fifteenth day comes a feast of seven days, when unleavened bread is eaten (verse 17). The first and seventh days are sacred assemblies with no regular work. On each of the seven days the priests offer two bulls, a ram and seven lambs, with a goat ‘to make atonement for you’ (verses 19-24).

Then, seven weeks later: “On the day of firstfruits, when you present an offering of new grain to the LORD during the Feast of Weeks, you are to hold a sacred assembly” (verse 26). The same offerings are made (verses 27-31).
passages.hearers:
The calendar now reaches the yearly feasts of spring. The first month, later called Nisan, falls in March or April. Passover remembered the night Israel left Egypt. The week of unleavened bread that followed recalled the haste of that leaving.

The chapter says almost nothing about the Passover meal itself, which families kept in their homes. Its interest is the altar. All through the week, on top of the daily lambs, the same large offering is made each day for the nation.

The Feast of Weeks came seven weeks later, at the end of the grain harvest in late spring. It is called here ‘the day of firstfruits’. The first of the new grain was brought to God before the people enjoyed the rest. In Greek the feast came to be called Pentecost, from the word for fiftieth.

Read aloud, the chapter is very repetitive: ‘unblemished’, ‘a pleasing aroma’, ‘in addition to the regular burnt offering’. The repetition is how the chapter teaches. Worship was meant to fill Israel's time, day after day and season after season.

Each feast includes one goat as a sin offering. Even on the days of greatest joy the people are reminded that they come to God as people who need atonement.
passages.later:
The Gospels place the death of Jesus at Passover, and Paul writes, “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The Spirit was given to the church at the Feast of Weeks: “When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place” (Acts 2:1).

Hebrews sets the repeated offerings of this calendar beside the one offering of Christ: “Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11-12). The New Testament makes these links itself, reading the calendar in the light of Christ. Jewish communities keep Passover and the Feast of Weeks, called Shavuot, to this day.
passages.asks: The first of the harvest went to God before anyone enjoyed the rest. Ask what comes first out of what you earn or receive. And ask which seasons of your year are marked by remembering what God has done, and which pass with no thought of him.
